name: Humpback Song
description: Oceanic song culture intelligence. Male humpback whales in a population sing the same song, which evolves collectively across a breeding season. New song variations originate in one ocean basin and propagate eastward across entire hemispheres over several years — a continent-scale cultural wave. Songs are hierarchically structured into units, phrases, themes, and complete arrangements, rivaling human musical grammar. One of the only non-human examples of culturally transmitted music at planetary scale.

core_attributes.pattern: global song propagation, hierarchical musical grammar, seasonal cultural evolution

scope.definition: Speed of novel song theme spread across Pacific Ocean humpback whale populations — measured as km/year wave velocity from point of origin (Australia) to Hawaii and North Pacific populations.

evidence.source: Garland et al. (2011) 'Dynamic horizontal cultural transmission of humpback whale song at the ocean-basin scale', Current Biology 21:687-691.
cross_domain_examples: novel song themes spread east across Pacific at estimated 800-1000 km/year transmission velocity
unidirectional spread (west to east) consistent with male-male cultural copying rather than shared breeding grounds
human pop music spread before internet: analogous one-directional cultural wave propagating at shipping-route speed

scope.falsifiability: If novel song themes appear simultaneously in geographically separated populations with no evidence of transmission path, independent invention rather than cultural wave propagation is the explanation.
scope.measurement_limits: Wave velocity is estimated from recording date and location of first appearance — propagation path is inferred. Transmission mechanism (direct contact vs indirect acoustic range) remains uncertain.

scope.definition: Number of distinct hierarchical levels (unit→phrase→theme→song) in humpback whale song structure, and the proportion of phrase transitions that follow statistical regularities (transition probability >80% for the most common next phrase).

evidence.source: Payne & McVay (1971) 'Songs of Humpback Whales', Science 173:585-597; Suzuki et al. (2006) 'Information entropy of humpback whale songs', Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 119:1849-1866.
cross_domain_examples: humpback song has 4-6 hierarchical levels with clear unit-phrase-theme-song segmentation
phrase transition entropy 1.4 bits vs maximum possible 3.2 bits — structured, not random sequence
human music: comparable 4-level hierarchy (note→motif→phrase→section) with similar transition probability structure

scope.falsifiability: If statistical analysis of long recording sequences shows transition probabilities between song units are uniformly distributed (maximum entropy), the hierarchical composition model is unsupported.
scope.measurement_limits: Hierarchical analysis requires minimum 3-5 hours of continuous recording per individual. Song structure changes seasonally (peak breeding complexity) and between years as songs evolve.

scope.definition: Rate of song change within a breeding season — fraction of phrases that are modified (note count, duration, frequency) between start-of-season (October) and end-of-season (March) recordings of same population.

evidence.source: Noad et al. (2000) 'Cultural revolution in whale songs', Nature 408:537-538; Cerchio et al. (2001) 'Interannual variation in songs of humpback whales', Animal Behaviour 62:943-956.
cross_domain_examples: Australian humpback song changes 30-50% of phrase types within a single 5-month breeding season
all males in population converge on same new phrases simultaneously — social synchronization of evolution
human language change: 0.5-2% vocabulary turnover per decade — cultural evolution at much slower rate

scope.falsifiability: If multiple season recordings show song unchanged between October and March, within-season song evolution is not occurring in that population.
scope.measurement_limits: Evolution rate is population-specific. Eastern Pacific populations show slower within-season change than Australian populations. Years with novel theme introduction (cultural revolution) show accelerated change.
